{"results":[{"id":"KB-C4","class":"contraception","title":"Do I still need a condom if I'm on the pill or the implant?","content":"Yes, if you want protection from STIs. Condoms are the only contraceptive method that prevents both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Other methods prevent pregnancy only, so Kenyan guidance strongly encourages young people to use condoms as well, for dual protection.

Evidence: Condoms are the only method that prevents both pregnancy and STIs including HIV; Kenyan guidance urges adolescents to use condoms for dual protection.

Conditions: Protection depends on using condoms consistently and correctly. Step-by-step use instructions are not included because no verified source text was reached.

Safety notes: If a condom breaks or slips, or she has had unprotected sex, she should see a health worker promptly. Emergency contraception timing is held for expert review. She should also go for any STI symptoms.","source":"WHO, Family planning/contraception methods fact sheet (3 July 2025); Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guidelines, 6th ed., p. 39","score":0.8840100765228271},{"id":"KB-C3","class":"contraception","title":"Which birth control methods can a teenager use?","content":"Kenya's national family planning guidelines say adolescents can safely use any contraceptive method, following the guidelines and the WHO eligibility criteria. A health worker will help you choose, and some medical conditions can change which method suits you. Using condoms as well gives extra protection against STIs.

Evidence: Kenyan guidance states that adolescents and youth can safely use any contraceptive method, applying the national guidelines and WHO medical eligibility criteria.

Conditions: Individual medical conditions change eligibility. Per-method eligibility categories are not stated because they could not be verified. The 7th edition (2025) of the Kenyan guidelines could not be read and may differ.

Safety notes: A health worker should confirm the choice, especially if she has a medical condition or might already be pregnant.","source":"Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guidelines for Service Providers, 6th ed., p. 39; WHO, Family Planning: A Global Handbook for Providers (2022), Ch. 1, p. 5","score":0.8543804883956909},{"id":"KB-C5","class":"contraception","title":"Will contraception make me infertile or stop me having babies later?","content":"No. WHO states that modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. After you stop a method your fertility comes back, though Kenya's guidelines say that for most methods it can take 3 to 6 months on average. Getting pregnant later is still possible.

Evidence: WHO: modern contraceptive methods do not cause infertility. Kenya: average 3 to 6 months delay in return to fertility for most methods.

Conditions: The delay before fertility returns varies by method and person. No method-specific figure (for example for injectables) was found in a source, so none is given. This does not address infertility caused by untreated STIs.

Safety notes: If she is worried about her fertility, or has pelvic pain or unusual discharge, she should see a health worker.","source":"WHO, Family planning/contraception methods fact sheet (2025); Kenya MoH, National Family Planning Guidelines, 6th ed., p. 45; WHO, Family Planning Handbook (2022), Ch. 1, p. 3","score":0.8404698371887207}]}

Conditions: The self-care advice comes from a UK source; no Kenyan source on period pain was found. No doses are given. Some painkillers are unsuitable for some people (for example with stomach ulcers or asthma), which was not verified in these sources.

Evidence: WHO: menstrual bleeding that is unpredictable, infrequent, very painful, heavy, or disrupts normal activities could suggest an underlying health condition. NHS: periods are more likely to be irregular when they first start in puberty.

Conditions: No numeric cycle-length range is given: the figures found (an NHS adult definition of under 21 or over 35 days) are not adolescent- or Kenya-specific, and no Kenyan source gave a range.

Safety notes: Very heavy bleeding, or pain that stops usual activities, needs a facility visit. A late period should be routed to a health worker or a pregnancy test, not diagnosed.","source":"WHO, Menstrual health fact sheet; NHS, Irregular periods (UK)","score":0.8600894212722778}]}

{"results":[{"id":"KB-S4","class":"sti","title":"I have unusual discharge, itching, burning or lower belly pain. Could it be an STI?","content":"It could be. Unusual discharge, genital sores or lower belly pain can be signs of an STI, but many STIs cause no symptoms at all, so only a test can tell. A health worker can examine you and give treatment, and Kenya's guidelines say providers must ensure privacy and confidentiality when serving adolescents.

Evidence: Lower abdominal pain, pain during sex, bleeding between periods and fever may indicate pelvic inflammatory disease; most STIs have no symptoms; providers must ensure privacy and confidentiality for adolescents.

Conditions: 2018 is the only Kenyan STI guideline edition found, read through a third-party copy. No treatment or drug advice is given.

Safety notes: Lower belly pain with fever, or pain during sex, needs a clinic visit soon. She should not self-treat.","source":"Kenya MoH, National Guidelines for Prevention, Management and Control of STIs (2018), s. 4.3 p. 39 and s. 4.5.4 p. 44; WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet","score":0.9058697819709778},{"id":"KB-S5","class":"sti","title":"Can STIs be cured, and can they harm me if I leave them?","content":"Four common STIs (syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis) can be cured with antibiotics. HIV and herpes cannot be cured, but medicine can keep them under control. Some untreated infections can spread and cause pelvic inflammatory disease, so it is better to get tested and treated early.

Evidence: Syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis are curable; HIV and herpes are not but can be managed; untreated infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease.

Conditions: Being cured does not protect against catching the infection again. Partner treatment and finish-the-course advice are not included because no verbatim source text was seen.

Safety notes: She should go to a clinic for testing and treatment rather than self-treating.","source":"WHO, Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet; Kenya MoH, STI guidelines (2018), s. 4.3 p. 39","score":0.8793106079101562},{"id":"KB-P6","class":"pregnancy","title":"What warning signs in pregnancy mean I should go to hospital right away?","content":"Kenya's Mother and Child Health Handbook lists these warning signs: vaginal bleeding, severe stomach pain, the baby moving less or not at all, fits, fever, a severe headache, waters breaking, and swelling of the face and hands. If you have any of them, go to a health facility straight away.

Evidence: The handbook lists these danger signs and advises being prepared to seek skilled care at a health facility for any of them.

Conditions: A lay list from the handbook, not a clinical triage protocol. An earlier (2016) copy lists a different set of signs, so use the 2020 edition.

Safety notes: Any of these signs means going to the nearest health facility immediately. She should not wait or treat at home.","source":"Kenya MoH, Mother & Child Health Handbook (Afya ya Mama na Mtoto), revised 2020","score":0.8672994375228882}]}

{"results":[{"id":"KB-G7","class":"general","title":"What does a youth-friendly health service offer, and what should I expect?","content":"Kenya's national guidelines say youth-friendly services should be accessible, acceptable, appropriate, effective and equitable: free or affordable, with providers who do not judge you. They should offer counselling on growth and development, relationships and sexuality, and services such as contraception counselling, pregnancy testing, and STI and HIV care. These can be found at health facilities, pharmacies, mobile clinics and help lines.

Evidence: Youth-friendly services are defined as accessible, acceptable, appropriate, effective and equitable; the package includes counselling on growth and development, relationships and sexuality; delivery points include facilities, pharmacies, mobile clinics and help lines.

Conditions: Written as what services 'should' offer: practice varies and a given facility may not offer everything. No verified facility directory, helpline or hours were found. The 2016 edition may have been superseded. Post-abortion care and sexual violence content in the guidelines is held and not used here.

Safety notes: Urgent symptoms (heavy bleeding, severe pain, possible pregnancy) need prompt care.","source":"Kenya MoH, National Guidelines for Provision of Adolescent and Youth Friendly Services in Kenya (2016), pp. 8, 18-19, 28-29, 34; Kenya MoH, National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy (2015), s. 6.2.3.6, p. 24","score":0.8807840347290039},{"id":"KB-G1","class":"general","title":"Will the clinic tell my parents what I talked to them about?","content":"Youth-friendly health services are expected to keep what you share confidential, including from parents — except in specific situations where the law requires disclosure, which staff should explain to you clearly.

Evidence: Providers must maintain confidentiality and not leak information to parents; legal exceptions exist but aren't specified in this source.

Conditions: Exact legal exceptions not established by this source — flag if a user's question implies a specific legal scenario.","source":"Kenya MoH YFS Guidelines (2005), Ch. 3 §3.2–3.3, pp. 16–17","score":0.8426030874252319},{"id":"KB-C1","class":"contraception","title":"Can I get birth control even though I'm a teenager?","content":"Health services for young people are meant to be confidential. The rules on parental consent for under-18s can differ by service, so a health worker can explain what applies to you. Specific service or legal requirements may vary by setting.

Evidence: WHO recommends adolescent SRH services, including contraceptive information and services, without mandatory parental/guardian authorization or notification.

Conditions: Consent wording is interim pending legal review (Children Act 2022 s.16(1)).","source":"WHO Recommendations (2018), Ch. 3 §3.3.2, p. 12","score":0.834754467010498}]}
